Conversion and division laboratory

The laboratory shows typed stages. It uses exact integer arithmetic for the unsigned storage demonstration and explicitly truncates the division model toward zero for the C comparison. It does not compile arbitrary C, model pointers, simulate undefined executions, or reproduce every platform's floating rounding rules. Select a case, adjust the inputs, and read both the result and its explanation. The lesson remains readable without JavaScript; the worked problems contain the same reasoning.

    For the initial storage example, the intermediate sum is 260 in int and the stored byte is four. Switching to division with negative inputs shows why memorizing “discard the remainder” is insufficient: the direction of quotient rounding determines the remainder's sign. A zero divisor is reported as a rejected operation; no fabricated numeric output is produced.

    Teaching through formulas and conceptual decisions

    Type the operands before evaluating the expression

    The language for the following questions is C17. Machine widths are specified whenever needed. Integer promotions occur before the usual arithmetic conversions. With 32-bit int and unsigned int, comparing -1 to 1u first converts the negative integer to the corresponding unsigned value, making the comparison false. This rule is not shared by every programming language and cannot be replaced by mathematical integer ordering.

    For division of two integer operands, compute the truncated integer quotient before assigning to a floating object. double z = 3/2; stores 1.0, while double z = (double)3/2; stores 1.5. Casting the already computed quotient cannot restore its discarded fractional part. C17 signed division truncates toward zero and its remainder satisfies a == (a/b)*b + a%b for defined operands.

    Distinguish storage width, promotion width and assignment conversion

    On an8-bit unsigned-character model, unsigned char x = 250; x += 10; computes the promoted sum 260 in an int that can represent it, then converts the assignment back modulo 256 to4. Unsigned arithmetic has modular semantics, but a narrow unsigned operand may be promoted to a signed int first. Therefore not every intermediate expression inherits the storage width of its variable.

    Classify behavior before predicting an output

    Unsigned wraparound is defined. Overflow of a signed arithmetic result is undefined, so an exam answer must not invent a wrapped numeric result. A C17 expression with unsequenced modification and access to the same scalar, such as i++ + i, is undefined. Precedence determines parsing, while sequencing determines which evaluations may legally interact. Short-circuit logical operators specify evaluation order and can suppress an otherwise invalid operation.

    For an IEEE binary64 exercise, exact integer representation extends through 253. At larger magnitudes, neighboring integers need not be distinct after conversion. This is a specified numeric model for those questions, not a guarantee that every C implementation uses binary64 for double.

    Detailed derivation tutorials

    The following complete proofs and implementations support the new examination problems. They develop the reasoning needed to derive formulas; the separately labeled examination bank below tests calculation, concepts and distractor decisions.

    Each problem gives its assumptions before its solution. The bank includes original questions and independently worded applications of explicitly identified course exercise patterns. It does not reproduce an entire course assignment or any archived Iranian paper. An undefined expression is classified without running it to guess a result. All code uses C17 unless another language is named.

    Tutorial 1 — Assignment stores a snapshot

    Task. Trace int x = 6, y = 9; int z = x + y; x = 2; y = z - x; and explain whether the final objects satisfy z == x + y by a lasting dependency.

    Solution. First record x = 6 and y = 9. The addition computes fifteen and stores it in z. Reassigning x stores two without recomputing z. Finally z - x uses fifteen and two, so y becomes thirteen. The final tuple is (2, 13, 15). It happens to satisfy the equality because the last assignment was constructed from z and x, not because a permanent relationship was installed. Replacing the last statement with y = 100 would immediately destroy that equality. This distinction prevents treating a program trace as simultaneous algebraic equations. Pattern: MIT Lecture 1, Bindings; all numbers and this explanation are original.

    Tutorial 2 — Copying is not swapping

    Task. Starting with int a = 4, b = 11;, compare a = b; b = a; with int t = a; a = b; b = t;.

    Solution. In the first sequence the first statement stores eleven in a, destroying a's old value. The second statement therefore copies eleven into b. Both end at eleven. In the second sequence t first preserves four. Reassigning a to eleven leaves t untouched; the last statement copies four into b. The final pair is (11, 4). The temporary object preserves information that would otherwise be lost. A swap expressed through arithmetic may overflow, while this version does not perform arithmetic. Pattern: Princeton §1.2, assignment and swap exercises.

    Tutorial 3 — Literal base changes type

    Task. Assume LP64, 32-bit int, and 64-bit long. Determine the types and values of 010, 0x10, 2147483648, 0x80000000, and 1.0f + 1.0.

    Solution. An initial zero makes 010 octal, so its value is eight and its type is int. Hexadecimal 0x10 is sixteen and also fits int. The decimal value 2147483648 exceeds INT_MAX; the next decimal candidate is signed long, which fits it. The hexadecimal value with the same magnitude fits the earlier hexadecimal candidate unsigned int. The suffix on 1.0f creates a float, while 1.0 is double; usual arithmetic conversions select double, and the result is the exact floating value two. Determine each literal's type before considering a destination.

    Tutorial 4 — Character code is not numeric value

    Task. With ASCII for this example, find the values and types of '7', '7' - '0', and a char c = '7'; promoted in c + 1.

    Solution. The character constant '7' has type int and ASCII value 55. Subtracting the code for '0', which is 48, gives seven in int. The char object stores 55; with the declared eight-bit character and 32-bit int model, its promotion preserves 55 and c + 1 computes 56 in int. That is the code for '8' under ASCII, but the expression is still integer arithmetic. The digit subtraction remains valid for decimal digits without assuming ASCII because their codes are contiguous by the C requirements.

    Tutorial 5 — sizeof does not increment this operand

    Task. For 32-bit int, int i = 7; size_t n = sizeof(i++);, determine n and i. Would replacing the operand with a variable-length-array type justify the same general rule?

    Solution. With an eight-bit byte and 32-bit int, the fixed-size operand has storage size four bytes. sizeof does not evaluate this i++, so n is four and i remains seven. The result's type is size_t, not int. The VLA case requires separate analysis because the size can depend on run-time bounds and relevant evaluation. Therefore “sizeof never evaluates anything” is too broad. This problem illustrates both the ordinary rule and the boundary that prevents an invalid generalization.

    Tutorial 6 — Promotion before byte storage

    Task. In the declared model, let unsigned char a = 250, b = 10; int s = a + b; unsigned char t = a + b;. Find both values and the expression type.

    Solution. Every possible value of either byte fits in int, so both operands promote to int. The mathematical sum 260 is representable in that expression type. Storing into s preserves it. Storing into t converts the already computed integer 260 modulo 256, giving four. The different destinations do not change the intermediate sum's type. The stored tuple is (260, 4). Calling the addition itself “eight-bit wrap” would misidentify the stage at which the reduction occurs.

    Tutorial 7 — Unary minus of a promoted unsigned byte

    Task. For unsigned char c = 1;, determine the type and value of -c and of (unsigned char)-c in the declared model.

    Solution. Unary minus first promotes c to int. Its negation is therefore the signed int value negative one, which is representable. The outer cast in the second expression converts that integer to an eight-bit unsigned value. Its residue is 255, because −1 ≡ 255 modulo 256. Thus the first expression is int negative one; the second is unsigned char 255. The operand's stored unsigned type does not bypass promotion.

    Tutorial 8 — General unsigned conversion

    Task. Find the residues of −513, −256, −1, 256, and 769 in an eight-bit unsigned destination. Prove one answer without appealing to a machine bit pattern.

    Solution. The required interval is zero through 255. The residues are respectively 255, zero, 255, zero, and one. For the first value, −513 = (−3)·256 + 255, so 255 lies in the allowed interval and is congruent to the source. Uniqueness of the interval representative proves the result. This calculation is an integer conversion; attempting the same argument for a floating source outside the destination's allowed integral range would be invalid.

    Tutorial 9 — Equal-rank signed and unsigned comparison

    Task. Under 32-bit int, evaluate -3 < 2U, -3 == (unsigned int)-3, and -3 > -4.

    Solution. The first comparison has equal-rank signed and unsigned operands, so negative three converts to unsigned int 4294967293. That is not less than two, and the comparison returns int zero. In the equality, both sides compare as unsigned int with the same value, so its result is int one. The final comparison has two signed int operands; negative three is greater than negative four, giving one. Signedness changes operand interpretation; it does not change comparison results into unsigned values. Pattern: Stanford CS107 Lecture 2, mixed-type comparisons.

    Tutorial 10 — The higher-rank signed range test

    Task. Evaluate -1L < 1U on LP64 and LLP64, both with 32-bit int. Explain why “unsigned always wins” is incorrect.

    Solution. long outranks unsigned int in both models. On LP64 its 64-bit signed range contains all 32-bit unsigned values, so the common type is signed long; negative one is less than one. On LLP64, signed long is 32-bit and cannot contain the entire unsigned int range. The common type becomes unsigned long, and negative one converts to its maximum, making the comparison false. The answer is true on LP64 and false on LLP64. Rank decides which range question to ask; range decides whether the higher signed type can prevail.

    Tutorial 11 — Conditional branches determine type together

    Task. With 32-bit int, determine the value and type of 1 ? -2 : 3U. Is the unsigned branch evaluated?

    Solution. The condition one is true, so only the middle branch's value is evaluated. However, the result type is chosen from both arithmetic branch types, int and unsigned int, yielding unsigned int. The selected negative two is converted to that type and becomes 4294967294. The unselected branch is not evaluated. Type determination and dynamic branch evaluation are different stages. Assigning this result to long long afterward preserves the large unsigned value rather than restoring negative two.

    Tutorial 12 — Cast placement in division

    Task. Compare double a = 9/4;, double b = (double)(9/4);, and double c = 9/(double)4;.

    Solution. The first two divisions use int operands and truncate to two. Conversion of that result yields 2.0, whether requested by assignment or by an explicit outer cast. The third division converts nine to double because the other operand is double; it computes 2.25. All three are defined, but only the third preserves the fractional quotient. The receiving type and an outer cast are too late to alter the division operator's operand types. Pattern: Harvard truncation example and Princeton §1.2 Web Exercise 5.

    Tutorial 13 — Four signs of quotient and remainder

    Task. Find (a/b, a%b) for the pairs (17, 5), (−17, 5), (17, −5), and (−17, −5), then check the identity.

    Solution. Truncation toward zero gives the tuples (3, 2), (−3, −2), (−3, 2), and (3, −2). For example, seventeen divided by negative five has quotient negative three; multiplying gives fifteen, leaving positive two. In every case bq + r equals a, and the remainder's absolute value is less than five. Its sign follows the dividend when nonzero, not the divisor. Python floor division for (−17, 5) instead gives (−4, 3), also satisfying its identity with a different quotient rule.

    Tutorial 14 — Ceiling without dangerous addition

    Task. For nonnegative int n and positive int d, show how to compute the number of d-item groups needed, including at n = INT_MAX. Explain why (n+d-1)/d can fail.

    Solution. Compute n/d + (n%d != 0). Euclidean division gives n = dq + r. If r is zero, q groups suffice; otherwise one additional group is required. At INT_MAX and d = 2, q is 1073741823, r is one, and the result is 1073741824, which fits. The alternative expression would add one to INT_MAX before dividing, causing signed overflow. If d is one, the correction is zero, so the safe expression never increments the maximum. This proof addresses the intermediate expression, not merely the final mathematical result.

    Tutorial 15 — A nonnegative residue from a signed remainder

    Task. For arbitrary representable integer a and positive representable integer m, compute the representative of a modulo m in zero through m−1 without risking an unnecessary large addition.

    Solution. First calculate int r = a % m;. Positive m excludes the negative-one quotient exception and zero division. If r is negative, add m; otherwise leave it unchanged. In the negative case, −m < r < 0, so zero < r + m < m and the addition fits. For a = −17 and m = 5, the first remainder is −2 and the corrected result is three. (a % m + m) % m unnecessarily adds m when the remainder is already nonnegative and can overflow for large m. The conditional correction has a proved range.

    Tutorial 16 — A wider destination cannot repair multiplication

    Task. Under 32-bit int and at least 64-bit long long, analyse int x = 50000; long long y = x * x; and give a correct repair.

    Solution. Both operands are int, so the product is computed in int. Its mathematical value is 2500000000, greater than 2147483647, so the original execution has undefined behavior. Assignment to long long happens after that invalid operation and cannot repair it. Use long long y = (long long)x * x;. The common type is now long long before multiplication. Its required range contains 2500000000, so the operation and storage are valid. An outer cast (long long)(x*x) is still too late. Pattern: Princeton §1.2 Web Exercise 6, with C17 classification replacing Java wrapping.

    Tutorial 17 — Unsigned source operands can overflow signed arithmetic

    Task. Under 16-bit unsigned short and 32-bit int, analyse unsigned short a = 60000, b = 60000; unsigned int p = a*b;.

    Solution. int represents every value of a 16-bit unsigned short, so both operands promote to int. Their product 3600000000 does not fit 32-bit signed int. The execution is undefined before storage into the unsigned destination. To obtain a defined unsigned 32-bit product here, convert an operand first: (unsigned int)a * b. The other promoted operand then converts to unsigned by the usual conversions, and 3600000000 lies below UINT_MAX. Larger inputs in another type might still wrap; the repair's range proof is specific to these source ranges.

    Tutorial 18 — Derive an addition guard

    Task. With a = 2147483640 and b = 20 in the 32-bit signed model, apply the chapter's overflow guard. Repeat with a = −2147483640 and b = −20.

    Solution. For positive b, INT_MAX - b is 2147483627. Since a exceeds it, reject the first sum without evaluating the sum. For negative b, INT_MIN - b is −2147483628. The second a is smaller than that threshold, so reject the second sum. Both threshold computations are representable. The guards are obtained by solving the appropriate upper- or lower-bound inequality; they do not rely on observing a wrapped result. A post-operation test would already execute undefined arithmetic.

    Tutorial 19 — Negation, division, remainder, and narrowing are different

    Task. Classify -INT_MIN, INT_MIN/-1, INT_MIN%-1, and conversion of UINT_MAX to int in the declared model.

    Solution. The first three have undefined behavior. Negation and division require the unavailable positive magnitude 2147483648; remainder shares the division's representable-quotient precondition even though its mathematical residue would be zero. The final integer-to-signed conversion is instead implementation-defined or raises an implementation-defined signal in C17. A common implementation yields negative one, but that is not a portable C17 answer. These expressions must not be grouped under a single vague word such as “overflow.”

    Tutorial 20 — Precedence tree with mixed operations

    Task. Evaluate 2 + 3 * 4 << 1 and (2 + 3) * (4 << 1) for int operands. Check every intermediate range.

    Solution. Multiplication binds before addition, and addition before shifting. The first tree is (2 + (3*4)) << 1: multiply to twelve, add to fourteen, then shift the nonnegative representable value to 28. In the second tree the sum is five and the inner shift is eight, so multiplication gives forty. Each value and doubled value fits int, and each shift count is within range. Grouping determines the different results; no issue of conflicting side effects arises because the operands are constants.

    Tutorial 21 — Chained comparisons are not interval membership

    Task. For int x = 100;, evaluate 10 <= x <= 20, and write the intended test.

    Solution. Left associativity parses the expression as (10 <= x) <= 20. The first comparison yields one, and one is at most twenty, so the expression is true despite x lying outside the intended interval. For any ordinary integer x, the first comparison yields zero or one and the final test still succeeds. The correct expression is 10 <= x && x <= 20, which is false for one hundred. Both expressions have result type int. Pattern: Princeton §1.2 Web Exercise 2; C accepts a misleading chain while Java rejects its operand types.

    Tutorial 22 — Logical and bitwise operations disagree

    Task. Compare 6 && 3, 6 & 3, 6 || 3, 6 | 3, 6 ^ 3, and !!6 != !!3.

    Solution. Six and three are both nonzero, so logical AND and logical OR each return one. Their low binary patterns are 110 and 011. Bitwise AND gives 010, which is two; bitwise OR gives 111, which is seven; XOR gives 101, which is five. Both normalized truths are one, so logical truth inequality gives zero. A nonzero bitwise XOR is not proof that exactly one operand was truthy. Distinguish numerical bit differences from Boolean differences.

    Tutorial 23 — A shift uses the promoted left width

    Task. For unsigned char c = 1;, evaluate c << 8, c << 31, 1U << 31, and 1U << 32 under the declared model.

    Solution. c promotes to 32-bit int, so the first shift count is valid and its product 256 is representable. The second count is within 32, but the signed product 2147483648 is not representable, so that expression is undefined. The unsigned literal in the third expression has 32-bit unsigned type, and its shift yields 2147483648 with a valid count. The fourth has an invalid count equal to the width, so it is undefined even though the left operand is unsigned. Count validity and result representability are separate checks.

    Tutorial 24 — Short-circuiting protects a division

    Task. With int d = 0, n = 8;, compare d != 0 && n/d > 2 with n/d > 2 && d != 0 and (d != 0) & (n/d > 2).

    Solution. The first expression evaluates the false left guard and skips the division; its result is zero. The second attempts division first and is undefined. The bitwise AND evaluates both required operands without a short-circuit guarantee, so division by zero is still attempted and undefined. Truth-table similarity cannot replace sequencing semantics. For arbitrary signed inputs, a complete safety guard must also exclude the minimum-integer divided by negative-one case.

    Tutorial 25 — Defined increment traces

    Task. Trace int i=2; int a=i++; int b=++i; int c=(i++,i);.

    Solution. The first initializer yields the old value two for a, then completes the update so i is three before the next full expression. Prefix increment raises i to four and yields four for b. In the comma expression, postfix increment's old result is discarded and its update completes before the right operand reads i. Therefore c is five and final i is five. The tuple (a, b, c, i) is (2, 4, 5, 5). All increments are representable, and the comma operator supplies the sequencing needed inside the final expression.

    Tutorial 26 — Reject a plausible output puzzle

    Task. For a fresh int i=2;, classify separately i++ + i, i = i++, printf("%d %d", i++, i++), and (i++, i+1).

    Solution. The first has an unsequenced update and a read of the same object; the second has conflicting unsequenced updates; the third has two unsequenced argument updates, since the separating comma is punctuation. All three are undefined in C17, and assigning an imagined evaluation order does not fix them. The final comma operator completes the update from two to three before computing the right operand, so it is defined and gives four, leaving i at three. These are separate experiments with a fresh initial state, not a combined trace.

    Tutorial 27 — Macro parentheses do not prevent duplicate effects

    Task. Let #define MIN(a,b) ((a)<(b)?(a):(b)). Starting from int i=3;, analyse int z=MIN(i++,10); and separately MIN(i++,i++).

    Solution. The first expansion is ((i++)<(10)?(i++):(10)). The comparison uses three and increments i to four. The conditional operator sequences that condition before the selected branch. Since three is less than ten, the branch yields four and increments i to five. Thus z is four and final i is five: the execution is defined but not the intended single evaluation. In the second expansion, the condition compares two unsequenced modifications of i and is already undefined. The remedy is to avoid effectful arguments or use a suitable function. Pattern: Berkeley C Syntax, macro evaluation; this analysis corrects the claim that a selected argument is always repeated.

    Tutorial 28 — Binary fractions and exactness

    Task. Decide whether the reduced rational values 3/8, 1/10, and 7/20 have finite binary expansions. Explain why a double can still approximate all three.

    Solution. Eight is a power of two, so three eighths terminates as binary 0.011. Ten and twenty have a factor five remaining in their reduced denominators, so neither other fraction terminates in base two. A finite binary format rounds a nonterminating value to a nearby representable number; existence of such an approximation is different from exact equality. Precision and exponent-range conditions still determine whether a particular rational fits exactly in a given format. The argument proves termination, not unlimited storage precision.

    Tutorial 29 — A lost integer unit at binary64 precision

    Task. Assume binary64 nearest-even conversions. For the exactly represented integer p = 253, predict converting p + 1 and p + 2 to double. Is an integer equality necessarily preserved by conversion?

    Solution. Around p on the higher-magnitude side, consecutive binary64 values are two units apart. The integer p + 1 is halfway between p and p + 2; ties-to-even chooses p, whose significand endpoint is even. The integer p + 2 is exactly representable and remains p + 2. Thus distinct integers p and p + 1 can become the same floating value. Converting before an equality can lose distinctions. This is a precision limitation within range, not overflow of a floating exponent.

    Tutorial 30 — Finite-precision associativity fails

    Task. Under the declared binary64 evaluation model, compare (a + b) + c with a + (b + c) for a = 1016, b = −1016, and c = 1.

    Solution. The first parenthesized sum cancels the equal opposite magnitudes exactly to zero, then adds one, giving one. In the second grouping, the unit is too small to change b after nearest-even rounding at its magnitude. The inner sum rounds to b, and adding a cancels it to zero. The different results arise from rounding at different intermediate nodes. The assumptions exclude excess precision and compiler reassociation; without them, a concrete C execution needs its own model. An exact-real algebra identity cannot justify this finite-precision rewrite.

    Tutorial 31 — Formatting is not a numeric cast

    Task. Explain printf("%d", 2.75), printf("%f", 2.75f), and printf("%zu", sizeof(int)).

    Solution. The first supplies double where the format requires an int, so it is undefined; %d does not truncate the argument. In the second, default variadic promotion changes the float argument to double, matching %f. In the third, the unsigned type size_t returned by sizeof matches %zu, regardless of whether its width equals that of an int. If the desired result is integer two, explicitly convert the representable finite value with (int)2.75 and pass that to %d.

    Tutorial 32 — An integrated expression audit

    Task. Under 32-bit int, evaluate unsigned char c=250; int x=-1; unsigned int u=1U; int r=(c+10>255) && (x<u); unsigned char t=c+10;.

    Solution. Promote c to int, add ten to obtain 260, and compare it with 255; the first logical operand is one. Because it is true, evaluate the second comparison. The equal-rank unsigned common type converts x to 4294967295, which is not less than u, so the second logical operand is zero. The conjunction gives r = 0. The separate final addition again computes 260 in int, then unsigned byte storage gives t = 4. The trace combines promotions, comparison result types, short-circuit choice, and a later storage conversion without any undefined arithmetic.

    Tutorial 33 — Python file output and rebinding

    Task. In a Python 3 script, consider type(8) followed by print(4.0-1); then x=4; y=x*3; x=9; print(y). Explain what is printed and whether x can later refer to a string.

    Solution. The bare type(8) expression computes a type object but the file execution does not automatically display it. The explicit first print emits 3.0. The next sequence computes and binds y to twelve before rebinding x to nine; its print emits 12. Assigning x="nine" later is permitted in Python because the name can be rebound to an object of another type. The corresponding C object cannot acquire a new declared type. Pattern: MIT Lecture 1, all three written questions: file output, assignment legality, and binding snapshots. In either language, an assignment target must be valid; Python permits xy=2 as an identifier assignment but not x*y=2 as an equation-solving request.

    Tutorial 34 — Formula translation with explicit types

    Task. A dimensionless ratio is a+bd for integers a = 5, b = 8, d = 4. Write C code preserving its fractional part. Then explain why double value = a + b / d; changes two aspects of the intended computation.

    Solution. Use double value = ((double)a + b) / d;. The early conversion causes the sum and quotient to be computed in double; the result is 3.25. The proposed expression instead groups as a + (b/d), because division binds before addition. That division is also integer division, giving two; adding five gives seven, then assignment yields 7.0. Correcting only grouping to (a+b)/d still leaves integer division and gives 3.0. Correcting only the destination type solves neither issue. This original problem consolidates the mathematical-translation patterns reviewed in Princeton §1.2.

    Tutorial 35 — Approximate equality need not be transitive

    Task. For the rule |x − y| ≤ 0.1 with exact real numbers, use x = 0, y = 0.075, and z = 0.15 to test transitivity. Explain the consequence for replacing equality in a grouping algorithm.

    Solution. The adjacent distances are both 0.075, which pass the tolerance. The endpoint distance is 0.15, which fails. Thus x can be approximately equal to y and y to z without x being approximately equal to z. Exact equality is transitive; this approximate relation is not. An algorithm that merges equality classes therefore needs a specified clustering policy or a genuine equivalence relation, rather than blindly substituting a tolerance check. The example uses exact reals to show that the issue is inherent in the criterion, not merely binary rounding.

    Tutorial 36 — A full safety precondition for signed division

    Task. In the two's-complement int model, build a logical condition that permits evaluating a/b, including all boundary cases, and trace it for (INT_MIN,-1), (8,0), and (8,-2).

    Solution. Use b != 0 && !(a == INT_MIN && b == -1). For the first pair, the divisor is nonzero but the inner conjunction is true, so its negation rejects the operation. For the second, the first guard is false and the rest need not establish permission. For the third, the divisor is nonzero and the exceptional pair is absent, so division is allowed and gives negative four. This condition must guard the actual evaluation, for example as the condition selecting an appropriate branch. Computing the quotient earlier and then examining the guard would not protect it.

    Mathematical constructions needed by the question bank

    1. A semantic contract precedes every calculation

    A bit pattern, an exact integer, a typed C value and a rounded floating value are different objects. In a hardware word, low-bit storage is a specified map from integers to residues. In a C expression, types, promotions, sequencing and exceptional cases determine whether an operation has a value at all. In an exact-real CHOP problem, truncation is defined independently of representability in a C destination. In a decimal calculator, rounding at each node uses decimal significance. In a binary format, spacing is controlled by binary significance. Do not join these models merely because all five may display similar numerals.

    For the numerical C examples, the declared contract is eight-bit bytes, no padding in the named 32-bit integer types, signed range from negative two to the thirty-first power through one less than that positive power, unsigned range zero through one less than two to the thirty-second power, and two's-complement signed representation. Exact-width typedefs are assumed available when named. These are examples, not a claim about every C17 target or the computer rendering this page. The public N1570 document is a C11 committee draft; it supplies the cited scalar rules retained in the chapter's C17 scope, and is not mislabeled as the published C17 standard.

    The following pipeline is a proof procedure. Parse the expression; identify each leaf's type; apply that operator's own promotion and conversion rules; establish sequencing and reachable operations; test each intermediate's domain; evaluate defined operations; apply destination conversion only when reached. A common type can be determined from an unselected conditional alternative, while a short-circuit operand can be skipped entirely. A complete trace therefore records both static type information and actual evaluation.

    2. Range, residues and destination conversion

    For a mathematical unsigned word with w value bits, the represented domain is 0≤u<2w. Integer-to-unsigned conversion chooses the unique residue r in this domain such that

    x=q2w+r,0≤r<2w.

    Euclidean division proves existence and uniqueness. At x=−129, an eight-bit destination gets127; a 32-bit destination gets4294967167. The same integer has different nonnegative residues under the two moduli. This does not mean a floating-to-unsigned conversion is permitted to wrap an arbitrary negative or large real value.

    Two's-complement positional decoding uses a negative weight for the sign position and positive weights below it. It proves the asymmetric endpoints and explains why negating the minimum can fail. Hardware low-bit addition can always be depicted under its own modular contract; undefined signed C addition must instead stop at a range violation. An expression such as a multiplication of narrow unsigned operands may first promote to signed int, so source signedness alone is not an overflow proof.

    3. Minimum record layout is an algorithm, not a universal sizeof fact

    Assume a declared ABI places each member at the earliest permitted aligned offset with no discretionary padding. Let member i have byte size si, alignment ai, and let ei−1 be the preceding end offset. Define

    oi=ai⌈ei−1ai⌉,ei=oi+si,e0=0.

    If record alignment is A, its minimum total size is

    S=A⌈ekA⌉.

    The gap oi−ei−1 is internal padding; S−ek is tail padding. Each formula follows by taking the least aligned position no earlier than the occupied end, then reserving every member byte. This also proves that the record cannot end before its last member.

    For widths 5,4,1, alignments 1,4,1, and record alignment four, the offsets are zero, eight and twelve. There are three internal padding bytes, thirteen occupied-or-interior bytes through the final member, and three tail bytes, giving size sixteen. Reordering the members to widths 4,5,1 puts them at zero, four and nine, ending at ten and rounding to twelve. Reordering can change ABI size but is not permission to reorder fields of an existing externally specified binary format. C permits additional unnamed padding, so alignment constraints alone do not force this minimal algorithm's result. Questions24–27 explicitly adopt this algorithm rather than pretending their original alignment-only wording was sufficient.

    4. Arrays, row stride and packed-bit storage measure different things

    An actual r -by- c array with element width b contains rc elements and occupies brc bytes. Row stride is bc, and element (i,j) begins at byte offset b(ic+j). These formulas describe a contiguous array of arrays; they do not describe separately allocated rows behind a pointer-to-pointer object. A declared array parameter is adjusted to a pointer, so its parameter sizeof measures a pointer while the pointed-to row type can still describe one full row.

    A packed format placing one flag in each consecutive bit of eight-bit bytes needs ⌈n/8⌉ bytes. Write n=8q+r and use q+1r>0. This proof supplies a safe computational form without adding seven near an unsigned maximum. Serialization specifies the byte/bit contract independently of implementation-defined C bit-field allocation. Member padding, array stride, pointer width and packed-byte count are not interchangeable quantities.

    5. Floating exactness and rounding are separate proofs

    For normal binary precision p, binade [2e,2e+1) has spacing 2e−p+1. All integers through 2p are exact, while 2p+1 is not; some larger powers of two remain exact within exponent range. At 2p, spacing below is one and spacing above is two. A nearest-even midpoint chooses the neighbor whose retained significand integer is even. Hence binary64 rounds 253+1 down to 253 but rounds 253+3 up to 253+4.

    An expression tree can round different intermediate values depending on grouping. In the authentic decimal example, both exact expression trees have sum435.003, but rounding each operation yields435.01 and435.00. Show every exact intermediate and its rounded replacement. A display rounded to two decimal places does not change the stored value's precision, and a comparison tolerance requires an application-specific absolute/relative error model rather than a universal epsilon.

    6. Ten fully worked transfer challenges

    These are independently authored extensions of the reviewed mechanisms, not copied course or official exam questions. Each answer states the additional machine contract it uses.

    Challenge A — An unsigned source can overflow signed multiplication. Under int32 and available uint16_t and uint32_t, let uint16_t u=65535;. Is uint64_t r=u*u; safe? Both operands promote to int because their full range fits. The exact product is

    655352=4294836225>2147483647.

    The signed multiplication is undefined before assignment; a wider destination does not repair it. Converting one operand first, (uint32_t)u*u, gives common unsigned32 arithmetic and the exact product4294836225, which fits its domain. That value can then widen safely. The cast's location is the repair.

    Challenge B — Integer and floating unsigned conversions disagree. Compare (unsigned int)-1, (unsigned int)-1.0 and (unsigned int)-0.75. Integer conversion gives4294967295 modulo the unsigned32 range. Floating conversion discards the fractional part and requires that integer to be representable: negative one is not, so the second conversion is undefined. The third truncates to zero, which is representable, so its result is zero. No blanket rule that every unsigned conversion wraps can solve all three.

    Challenge C — Rank needs a range test. Let long s=-1; unsigned int u=1;. Under a declared LP64 model with signed long64 and unsigned int32, long has higher rank and represents every unsigned32 value, so the comparison s<u is signed and true. Under a declared LLP64 model with signed long32 and unsigned int32, long cannot represent that entire unsigned range, so the common type is unsigned long32. Negative one converts to4294967295 and the comparison is false. The host operating system is irrelevant to this two-model proof.

    Challenge D — Sequencing is a relation, not precedence. Starting independently with int i=1;, classify i++ + i++, (i++, i++) and i++ && i++. The plus operands' modifications are unsequenced, so no numeric output is specified. The comma operator sequences its left increment before its right: the returned right old value is two and the final stored value is three. Logical AND sequences the first operand, which returns one and is true, then evaluates the second, which returns two and is true; the logical result is one and final i is three. All increments here fit. Commas separating function arguments are not this comma operator.

    Challenge E — Parentheses cannot repair repeated side effects. For #define SQR(x) ((x)*(x)), expanding SQR(i++) produces two increments with no sequencing relation between multiplication operands. It is undefined even though grouping is correct. A function receiving i++ once instead captures one old value; starting at one, the call's scalar argument is one and i becomes two. Squaring that local one returns one. For larger inputs, the function still needs a square-range check.

    Challenge F — A representable final mathematical result is insufficient. In int32, take n=1073741824. The mathematical value −(2n)=−2147483648 fits, but 2*n first tries to produce2147483648 in int, which does not fit. The original expression is undefined. With a declared signed type able to represent both intermediate magnitudes, converting n to that type before multiplication makes the path valid; conversion of the final value to int32 is then permitted. A cast around the already-computed product is too late.

    Challenge G — Unsigned shifts still have domains. Under unsigned32/int32, 1u<<31 is2147483648; 1u<<32 is undefined because the count equals the promoted left width. 1<<31 is undefined in the C17 rule used here because the signed mathematical product does not fit int. Right-shifting a negative signed operand is implementation-defined. Each shift promotes its operands individually and retains the promoted left type; usual arithmetic conversions do not supply a common shift type.

    Challenge H — Two binary64 ties choose different directions. Let a=253. The midpoint a+1 has neighbors a,a+2, whose significand integers are 252 and 252+1. The lower is even, so it is selected. The midpoint a+3 has neighbors a+2,a+4, with odd and even significands respectively, so the upper is selected. The resulting values are a and a+4, under rounding of each operation to binary64. Midpoint parity explains both without executing potentially different host evaluation rules.

    Challenge I — Trace both internal and tail padding. For the three-member minimum ABI in section3, member widths5,4,1 yield offsets0,8,12 and end13. Record alignment four rounds13 to16. Reordering as4,5,1 yields offsets0,4,9, end10 and size12. The saved four bytes are not a missing member: the total member widths remain ten, while total padding changes from six to two. Identify every padding interval, rather than guessing one fixed amount per record.

    Challenge J — Allocation arithmetic needs guards before multiplication. Let unsigned size_t maximum be M, positive row count n and four-byte elements. The desired mathematical size is 4n(n+1). First reject n=M before adding one. Let c=n+1. Check c≤⌊M/4⌋, then form safe row size r=4c. Check n≤⌊M/r⌋, then form total nr. Both divisions have positive divisors. Every multiplication is now proved within range before it executes. A wrapped small count is not evidence that the intended large array fits; a successful representability check also does not guarantee allocation succeeds.

    7. Four freshly reviewed university roles and exercise coverage

    Harvard CS50x2025 provides declaration, expression and truncation examples. Berkeley CS61C's written scalar sections provide portability, initialization and macro issues. Princeton COS126 §1.2 provides value/operation structure, Java contrasts, IntOps/DoubleOps examples and all48 displayed exercise statements in the accessible inventory. MIT6.0001 Fall2016 Lecture1 pages23–34 and its three written in-class questions provide Python objects, conversions, output and assignment snapshots. The language boundaries and corrected course generalizations are incorporated in the original exposition above and the retained tutorials. Princeton's image-only tables were inaccessible; their contents are not claimed read. Stanford CS107's earlier reading remains historical evidence because its renewal was unavailable. These four fresh roles were reassessed within the recorded bounded seven-offering pool, not selected randomly or proclaimed a global optimum.

    The original course exercise inventory is a source map, not a claim that every course's full exercise bank is reproduced here. Introductory expression/assignment exercises are represented by the retained tutorials; the authored challenges extend promotions, signed domains, sequencing, layout and floating error. Whole course syllabi extend beyond this chapter boundary. Advanced C claims are cross-checked against the language reference and independent derivations because an introductory course combination alone cannot establish them.

    Authentic examination questions

    The authentic items below test numeric primitives, precision, and encoding; they do not claim to be C17 type-system questions. The original questions make the language rules explicit.

    Question 1. PhD CE 1405, Q31 — Four-bit signed overflow

    Authentic examination · English translation

    Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 31. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

    Using four-bit two's-complement numbers, which addition overflows?

    1.

    0101 + 1000

    2.

    0010 + 0101

    3.

    0100 + 1110

    4.

    1100 + 1011

    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 4. This is a four-bit hardware representation question, not an instruction to execute overflowing signed C arithmetic.

    Decode, add mathematically, then test the range

    A four-bit two's-complement pattern has weights −8,4,2,1. Its signed domain is [−8,7]. For example, 1100=−8+4=−4 and 1011=−8+2+1=−5. Checking all four alternatives gives:

    Option Decoded operands Mathematical sum Low four bits Signed overflow?
    1 5,−8 −3 1101 No
    2 2,5 7 0111 No: the endpoint is included.
    3 4,−2 2 0010 No
    4 −4,−5 −9 0111 Yes: −9<−8.

    In the last addition, low-bit storage computes 12+11=23=16+7. Discarding the fifth bit leaves the pattern for positive seven. That bit pattern cannot represent the correct signed answer. Both negative operands produced a nonnegative stored result, the characteristic signed-overflow condition. Equivalently, the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out. Unsigned carry and signed overflow answer different questions: option 3 has an unsigned carry although its signed result is valid; option 2 can overflow neither interpretation.

    Derive the general test

    Opposite-sign operands sum between the two inputs, so cannot leave the signed range. Two nonnegative operands can exceed the upper endpoint; two negative operands can fall below the lower endpoint. Test the exact mathematical sum against both endpoints before interpreting low bits. For a C17 expression evaluated in a signed type, an unrepresentable result has undefined behavior; two's-complement storage does not authorize predicting a wrapped C output. This distinction prevents a correct hardware calculation from becoming an incorrect language answer.

    This model declares its language or representation contract and uses the actual question data.

    Question 2. MSc CS 1393, Q165 — Truncation is not decimal rounding

    Authentic examination · English translation

    Original booklet · PDF page 33 · question 165. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

    CHOP removes the fractional part of a real number, truncating toward zero. Which statement is false?

    1.

    If x is an integer, x=CHOP(x).

    2.

    If x<0, CHOP(x−0.5) rounds x to an integer.

    3.

    If x≥0,

    CHOP(100x+0.5)/100

    rounds x to two decimal places by truncation.

    4.

    If x≥0, CHOP(100x)/100 truncates x to two decimal places.

    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 3. The false description equates rounding with truncation. The formula itself performs rounding under the stated exact-real model.

    Start from the definition of CHOP

    For an exact real t, truncation toward zero is

    t≥0⇒CHOP(t)=⌊t⌋,t<0⇒CHOP(t)=⌈t⌉.

    Every integer therefore remains unchanged, establishing option 1. For a negative x, subtracting one half before truncation implements nearest-integer rounding, with ties away from zero: at x=−2.49 the intermediate is −2.99 and the result −2; at x=−2.5 the intermediate is −3 and the result −3. This is the tie convention implicit in option 2, rather than ties to even.

    For nonnegative x, scaling by one hundred moves the hundredths digit into the integer position. At x=1.239 the two relevant calculations are

    CHOP(123.9)100=1.23,CHOP(123.9+0.5)100=1.24.

    Adding one half decides which hundredth is nearest; it does not merely remove all digits beyond the hundredths place. Hence option 3's claim of truncation is false, while option 4 correctly describes truncation. At the halfway input 1.235, the offset formula returns 1.24, clarifying its upward tie rule for positive inputs. The extension to x=0 also works, although it is not needed to broaden the original source's domain.

    Keep the mathematical primitive separate from a C cast

    CHOP is defined here for all exact real arguments. A C floating-to-integer conversion first discards the fraction but additionally requires the resulting integer to fit the destination. Binary approximation of 100x can move a intended decimal halfway value slightly to either side. Thus this proof neither authorizes an out-of-range C cast nor guarantees exact decimal rounding for every double. Identify the arithmetic and tie model before applying a memorized offset formula.

    This model declares its language or representation contract and uses the actual question data.

    Question 3. MSc CS 1404, Q51 — Finite precision breaks associativity

    Authentic examination · English translation

    Original booklet · PDF page 11 · question 51. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

    A decimal floating-point calculator rounds each operation to four digits after the decimal point in a normalized mantissa. Let a=3.4127×102, b=8.1316×101, and c=1.2417×101. It computes A=(a+b)+c and B=a+(b+c). What is A−B?

    1.

    0.01

    2.

    0

    3.

    0.003

    4.

    -0.01

    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 1. The difference is 0.01, caused by two distinct intermediate-rounding paths.

    Determine the actual precision

    One digit before the normalized mantissa's decimal point plus four after it gives five significant decimal digits. Convert the inputs to ordinary notation:

    a=341.27,b=81.316,c=12.417.

    Write R(t) for rounding t to five significant decimal digits. The calculator evaluates A=R(R(a+b)+c) and B=R(a+R(b+c)), not one common exact sum followed by one final round.

    Node Exact operation on its current inputs Rounded output
    Left branch, first addition 341.27+81.316=422.586 422.59
    Left branch, second addition 422.59+12.417=435.007 435.01
    Right branch, first addition 81.316+12.417=93.733 93.733
    Right branch, second addition 341.27+93.733=435.003 435.00

    The final subtraction is exact at the available precision:

    A−B=435.01−435.00=0.01.

    None of these rounding decisions is a halfway case, so differences between nearest-even and nearest-away tie handling do not change this item.

    Explain every competing result

    Zero comes from importing the associativity of exact real addition into a machine that rounds after each operation. The value 0.003 is the exact total's discarded tail, not the difference of the two rounded expression trees. The value −0.01 reverses the requested subtraction. Counting only four significant digits also defines a different calculator from the source's normalized mantissa.

    The left branch introduces error 0.004 at its first node and then rounds again; the right branch's first node is already exact. This makes the mechanism visible instead of merely asserting that floating arithmetic is inaccurate. Always draw or record the evaluation tree, propagate each rounded output into the next operation, and preserve the stated decimal format. Replacing this machine with binary64 would answer another question.

    This model declares its language or representation contract and uses the actual question data.

    Question 4. Promote before complementing a narrow object

    Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

    Original authored typed-expression or representation question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

    In C17, unsigned char u=0x0F; CHAR_BIT=8 and int is 32-bit two's complement. What are the values of ~u and (unsigned char)~u?

    1.

    -16 and 240.

    2.

    240 and 240.

    3.

    -16 and -16.

    4.

    15 and 240.

    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 1. The intermediate expression has value −16 and type int; the separately converted unsigned character has value 240.

    Trace a typed value through three stages

    The eight-bit object stores u=15. Since every possible unsigned char value 0,…,255 fits the declared 32-bit int, integer promotion converts the operand to int before unary complement. The operator therefore complements the promoted pattern, not an isolated eight-bit byte. In the specified two's-complement representation,

    bitnot(15)=−15−1=−16.

    Converting this integer to the eight-bit unsigned destination selects its nonnegative residue:

    −16=(−1)256+240,(unsigned char)(bitnot(u))=240.
    Stage Type Value
    Stored source unsigned char 15
    Promoted operand int 15
    Complemented expression int −16
    Explicit narrowing destination unsigned char 240

    The alternative (240,240) incorrectly truncates the expression to eight bits before giving its first value. The pair (−16,−16) gives an impossible negative value to an unsigned destination. The pair (15,240) leaves the intermediate operand unchanged.

    Boundary and transfer

    For this model, source u=0 produces intermediate −1 and final 255; source u=255 produces intermediate −256 and final zero. These checks expose the difference between expression width and storage width. The identity bitnot(v)=−v−1 uses the stipulated two's-complement representation, rather than all historically permitted C17 signed representations. The unsigned destination's modulo conversion is a language rule; the signed complement's numerical interpretation additionally uses this declared representation. Neither stage is signed arithmetic overflow.

    This model declares its language or representation contract and uses the actual question data.

    Question 5. Integer division with casts at three locations

    Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

    Original authored typed-expression or representation question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

    In C17, let int a=7,b=3;. Which values belong to (double)(a/b), (double)a/b, and a/(double)b, respectively?

    1.

    2, 7/3, 7/3.

    2.

    7/3, 7/3, 7/3.

    3.

    2, 2, 7/3.

    4.

    2, 7/3, 2.

    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 1. The values are 2.0 and two floating approximations to 7/3. An outer cast cannot recover a discarded remainder.

    Compare the three expression trees

    For integer operands a=7,b=3, C17 integer division yields quotient two and remainder one:

    7=2·3+1.

    In (double)(a/b), the division node receives two integers. It returns integer two; only the parent cast changes that value's type to double. The final value is exactly 2.0 in the declared format.

    In (double)a/b, the left leaf becomes double seven before the division. The usual arithmetic conversions change integer three to double three, so the division is floating. In a/(double)b, converting the right leaf triggers the same common type and the same floating operation. Under the chapter's binary64 nearest-even model, both produce the same stored approximation to 7/3; the exact fraction is not representable in finite binary precision because its denominator includes a factor other than two.

    Expression Division operand types Division result before any outer action
    (double)(a/b) int, int Integer 2
    (double)a/b double, double Rounded approximation to 7/3
    a/(double)b double, double The same approximation

    Option 2 wrongly makes the first division floating. Option 3 ignores the conversion of the left operand in the second expression. Option 4 ignores the conversion of the right operand in the third. Assigning a/b into a double destination has the same lost-remainder problem as the first expression. For a general integer pair, first verify a nonzero divisor and a representable integer quotient; only then compare cast placement. The destination declaration does not retroactively determine a child operation's type.

    This model declares its language or representation contract and uses the actual question data.

    Question 6. A mixed-signedness conditional changes a value

    Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

    Original authored typed-expression or representation question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

    In C17 with 32-bit int and unsigned int, evaluate int x=-1; unsigned int y=1; followed by (1 ? x : y) > 2u.

    1.

    0

    2.

    1

    3.

    Undefined behavior.

    4.

    It depends on which branch executes.

    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 2. The comparison yields integer one. The selected source value is converted to an unsigned common type before comparison.

    Separate static typing from runtime selection

    The alternatives x and y have equal-rank int and unsigned int types. Applying the usual arithmetic conversions gives the conditional expression type unsigned int.     Question 12. A width-explicit unsigned range — exact instance 1

    Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

C guarantees at least the mandated minimum ranges, not the same exact width for every integer name on every implementation.     Question 16. A modular register addition with a carry out — exact instance 1

    Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

    Original authored typed-expression or representation question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

    In an unsigned (n+3) -bit modular register, add n+1 to the maximum value. Find the stored result. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 1.

    Construct the value and state its domain

    Let M=2n+3 be the modulus. The largest register value is M−1. Addition of n+1 gives

    s=(M−1)+(n+1)=M+n.

    Low-width storage retains the nonnegative residue of s modulo M. For every positive integer n, 2n≥n+1, as proved by induction: it holds at one, and doubling n+1 is at least n+2. Hence n<M and

    s=1·M+n,smodM=n.

    Exactly one modulus is discarded in this family. The carry is not a minus sign; the stored unsigned residue remains nonnegative.

    The unreduced expression 2n+3+n is the mathematical sum, not the register contents. The value n+1 fails to include the initial maximum's residue −1. The value −n is a sign mistake with no basis in unsigned reduction. Always distinguish exact total, discarded carry and stored result.

    A narrow C object can follow a different intermediate route. An eight-bit unsigned source 255 can promote to 32-bit signed int; adding six yields the representable expression value 261, and only assigning to an unsigned byte produces five. The hardware register and this typed C expression reach the same stored byte through different semantic checkpoints. A sufficiently large multiplication of promoted narrow unsigned sources can even overflow signed int, despite the source objects being unsigned.

    Requested instance or boundary

    At n=5, M=256 and 255+6=261=256+5, so option 1 stores five. The displayed 261 is the exact total; six is only the addend; negative five is outside the unsigned domain.

    Original authored typed-expression or representation question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

    A two’s complement signed representation has n value-and-sign bits with no padding. Find its minimum value. Calculate the requested quantity for n=8.

    1.
    −127
    2.
    0
    3.
    −128
    4.
    −256
    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 3.

    Construct the value and state its domain

    In an n -bit two's-complement representation, assign weight −2n−1 to the sign bit and positive weights 2j to lower positions. A pattern has value

    v=−bn−12n−1+∑j=0n−2bj2j.

    To minimize it, set the sign bit and clear every positive contribution. Therefore vmin=−2n−1. To maximize it, clear the sign bit and set every lower position, giving vmax=2n−1−1. The range contains 2n distinct integers and is asymmetric by one.

    The competing −2n requires an extra sign-weight position. The expression −(2n−1−1) omits the actual most-negative pattern; it is merely the negative of the positive maximum. Zero ignores every negative pattern. These distinctions follow directly from positional weights.

    Negating the minimum has mathematical result 2n−1, which exceeds the same-width signed maximum. If negation is evaluated in a signed type whose minimum is this value, as in -INT_MIN, it is undefined. A narrow signed source may first promote to a wider int; for signed char negative128 under int32, unary minus then yields representable int128. Converting that result back to signed char is a separate out-of-range signed conversion, with an implementation-defined result or signal. A cast afterward cannot repair an operation that already overflowed; an actual promotion or widening before the operator can change its domain. The two's-complement premise is essential to this endpoint pair, rather than a universal historical C17 representation guarantee.

    Requested instance or boundary

    For n=8, pattern 10000000 represents −128 and 01111111 represents 127. The negative endpoint is therefore option 3. Mathematical negation of −128 would require positive 128, unavailable in this same range.

    Padding under an explicitly specified layout

    Question 24. Padding under an explicitly specified layout — exact instance 1

    Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

    Original authored typed-expression or representation question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

    A record has a first member occupying n bytes, followed by a four-byte member requiring four-byte alignment. The record also requires four-byte alignment. Find total size under this layout. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

    Use the minimum-layout ABI: place the first member at offset zero and every subsequent member at its earliest aligned offset, insert no discretionary padding, and round the final size to record alignment. Alignment constraints alone would not make the answer unique.

    1.
    9
    2.
    8
    3.
    13
    4.
    12
    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 4.

    Construct the value and state its domain

    Use the explicitly repaired minimum-layout policy: the first member begins at offset zero, each following member occupies the earliest aligned offset, no extra discretionary padding is inserted, and final size is rounded to record alignment. Without this policy the stated widths and alignments alone do not force a unique C structure size.

    After the first n bytes, the next member must start at a multiple of four at least n. Its earliest offset is

    o=4⌈n4⌉.

    It occupies bytes o through o+3, so the end offset is o+4. This is already divisible by four, giving minimum size

    S=4⌈n4⌉+4.

    Write n=4q+r, 0≤r<4. Internal padding is zero if r=0 and 4−r otherwise; it varies from zero to three bytes. This residue proof explains the ceiling and rules out assuming a constant padding count.

    The expression n+4 ignores required internal padding whenever r≠0. The expression 4⌈n/4⌉ stops at the second member's starting offset and omits its storage. The expression n+8 assumes four padding bytes, which minimum alignment never requires here. Alignment adds unused positions; it does not erase member bytes.

    C permits extra unnamed internal or tail padding, so an ABI's precise policy, member alignment, packing directives and record alignment must be specified before a numerical sizeof claim. This solution computes the declared minimal model, not an implementation-independent size.

    Requested instance or boundary

    For n=5, occupied first-member offsets are 0…4, padding is 5…7, and the second member is 8…11. Size is twelve, option 4. A layout putting that member at offset twelve and ending at sixteen also satisfies alignment, showing why the new minimum-policy premise is necessary.

    This model declares its language or representation contract and uses the actual question data.

    Actual array storage rather than a decayed pointer

    Question 28. Actual array storage rather than a decayed pointer — exact instance 1

    Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

    Original authored typed-expression or representation question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

    A real two-dimensional array has n rows and n+1 columns, with four-byte elements and no padding between elements. Find its total byte size. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

    1.
    24
    2.
    30
    3.
    120
    4.
    20
    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 3.

    Construct the value and state its domain

    An actual two-dimensional array has n rows and n+1 elements per row. Arrays contain their elements contiguously; each row occupies 4(n+1) bytes and all rows occupy

    N=n(n+1)elements,S=4n(n+1)bytes.

    At zero-based element (i,j), the byte offset from the array start is 4(i(n+1)+j), for 0≤i<n and 0≤j<n+1. The final element begins at S−4 and ends at S−1, independently checking the total.

    The alternative 4n accounts for only one four-byte element per row. The expression 4(n+1) is one row's stride, not the complete array. The expression n(n+1) counts elements and leaves out their four-byte unit. A correct dimensional calculation keeps counts and bytes distinct.

    In most value contexts, an array expression converts to a pointer to its first element. sizeof on the actual array is an important exception. A function parameter declared with array syntax is adjusted to a pointer type at declaration time; its sizeof therefore measures that pointer object, not the pointed-to allocation. For a two-dimensional parameter, the pointed-to row type can still preserve its column count. sizeof a[0] can be a row size even when sizeof a is pointer size. Neither pointer width nor the number of rows alone recovers the allocated byte count. The positive dimensions here avoid zero-length standard-array declarations; real allocation arithmetic must separately guard against overflow.

    Requested instance or boundary

    For n=5, there are 5·6=30 elements; row stride is twenty-four bytes and full size 5·24=120, option 3. The last element (4,5) begins at 4(4·6+5)=116 and occupies bytes 116…119.

    This model declares its language or representation contract and uses the actual question data.

    Ceiling division for an explicit packed format

    Question 32. Ceiling division for an explicit packed format — exact instance 1

    Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

    Original authored typed-expression or representation question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

    A serialized format stores n Boolean flags in consecutive bits of eight-bit bytes, using the minimum whole-byte count. Find the byte count. Calculate the requested quantity for n=9.

    1.
    9
    2.
    72
    3.
    3
    4.
    2
    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 4.

    Construct the value and state its domain

    Divide the positive number of flags by eight:

    n=8q+r,0≤r<8.

    The first q bytes are full. If r=0, they hold every flag and no further byte is required. If r>0, at least one more whole byte is needed and is sufficient. Thus

    B=q+1r>0=⌈n8⌉.

    This is a minimality proof: B−1 bytes have fewer than n positions whenever B>0. The unused final-bit count is 8B−n, between zero and seven. A partial final byte cannot be omitted merely because some of its positions are unused.

    The distractor n stores one flag per whole byte, a different format. The quantity 8n is neither the required bytes nor the number of stored flags; it mixes a byte's capacity with the count. The expression ⌈n/8⌉+1 always allocates a redundant extra byte, including at exact byte boundaries.

    For a nonnegative integer n in a finite unsigned type, compute n/8 + (n%8 != 0) instead of blindly evaluating (n+7)/8: the latter addition can wrap near the unsigned maximum. The quotient form has room for its final possible increment when the divisor is eight. This is a serialization contract, not a C bit-field allocation guarantee. C bit-field units, order and padding require implementation information; an array of Boolean objects is also not this packed format.

    Requested instance or boundary

    For n=9, q=1,r=1. The first byte holds eight flags and the second holds one flag plus seven unused positions. Minimum size is two, option 4. Eight positions are insufficient; three bytes are unnecessary.

    This model declares its language or representation contract and uses the actual question data.

    ⌈n/8⌉+1
    2.
    ⌈n/8⌉
    3.
    n
    4.
    8n
    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 2.

    Construct the value and state its domain

    Divide the positive number of flags by eight:

    n=8q+r,0≤r<8.

    The first q bytes are full. If r=0, they hold every flag and no further byte is required. If r>0, at least one more whole byte is needed and is sufficient. Thus

    B=q+1r>0=⌈n8⌉.

    This is a minimality proof: B−1 bytes have fewer than n positions whenever B>0. The unused final-bit count is 8B−n, between zero and seven. A partial final byte cannot be omitted merely because some of its positions are unused.

    The distractor n stores one flag per whole byte, a different format. The quantity 8n is neither the required bytes nor the number of stored flags; it mixes a byte's capacity with the count. The expression ⌈n/8⌉+1 always allocates a redundant extra byte, including at exact byte boundaries.

    For a nonnegative integer n in a finite unsigned type, compute n/8 + (n%8 != 0) instead of blindly evaluating (n+7)/8: the latter addition can wrap near the unsigned maximum. The quotient form has room for its final possible increment when the divisor is eight. This is a serialization contract, not a C bit-field allocation guarantee. C bit-field units, order and padding require implementation information; an array of Boolean objects is also not this packed format.

    Requested instance or boundary

    Option 2 follows from quotient and remainder in both cases. At n=8 the answer is one, at nine two, at sixteen two and at seventeen three. These boundary transitions explain why unconditional quotient-plus-one is wrong. The extension to zero returns zero without allocating a fictitious partial byte.

    Question 36. The endpoint of consecutive integer exactness — exact instance 1

    Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

    A binary floating representation has n significant bits including its leading bit, with enough exponent range. Find the largest nonnegative integer up to which all consecutive integers are exact. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

    32

    31
    3.

    Read the full typed derivation, checks, and option analysis

    Correct option: 1.

    Construct the value and state its domain

    Let p=n significant binary bits include the leading bit, and assume adequate exponent range for every number under discussion. Any positive integer below 2p has at most p binary digits and can be represented exactly. The endpoint 2p itself is a power of two, requiring only one nonzero significand digit, so it is also exact.

    In binade [2e,2e+1), normal values have spacing

    Δe=2e−p+1.

    At e=p, the spacing is two. The integer 2p+1 lies halfway between 2p and 2p+2 and is not a representable value. Therefore the last endpoint through which every consecutive nonnegative integer is exact is 2p. This proves both inclusion and maximality.

The value p mistakes a count of significand bits for a numeric endpoint. More exponent range permits larger magnitudes but does not fill the missing significand positions.

    Some larger integers remain exact: 2p+2, 2p+1 and suitable larger powers of two within exponent range. Thus this is not the largest finite value or the largest exact integer. For nearest-even rounding at the midpoint, inspect significand parity; exactness and rounding of a nonrepresentable integer are different questions. Subnormal spacing near zero and finite exponent endpoints need their own premises; the present question explicitly supplies enough exponent range.

    Requested instance or boundary

    At p=5, integers zero through32 are exact. Just below32 the spacing is one; above32 the values are32,34,36 and so on. Thirty-three is missing, so option 1's32 is the endpoint. Thirty-one is too small; sixty-four is exact itself but not all intervening integers are exact.

    Question 40. Truncation toward zero versus floor — exact instance 1

    Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

    Using C17 signed integer division, divide −(3n+1) by 3; all values fit the chosen signed type. Find the quotient. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

    Construct the value and state its domain

    The exact mathematical dividend is a=−(3n+1) and the divisor is positive three. Its real quotient is

    a3=−n−13.

    C17 signed integer division discards the fractional part toward zero, giving q=−n. The remainder is determined from reconstruction:

    r=a−3q=−(3n+1)+3n=−1,a=3q+r.

A nonzero divisor alone is not enough for all signed inputs: INT_MIN/-1 has an unrepresentable quotient, and INT_MIN%-1 is undefined as well, even though its mathematical remainder is zero. First prove the operation's domain; only then use quotient/remainder identities. No simulator should return a numeric C result for an undefined boundary.
